---
title: "Updating the metadata on Zenodo"
description: |
  Use the `update` command to update metadata on an existing Zenodo deposit without changing its files or DOI.
order: 3
---

Have you published a record on Zenodo but afterwards discovered a typo, need to
correct information, or want to add missing metadata after publishing a deposit?

Instead of making a new record, you just want to update the metadata without
having to upload the files again or create a new DOI.

The `update` command updates the metadata of an existing Zenodo deposit based on
the `.zenodo.toml` file.

::: {.callout-caution}
Note that `update` requires an existing Zenodo deposit. If no deposit exists,
the command will fail. The deposit must first be published as a record (see [the
*publishing a record* guide](publishing.qmd)) before its metadata can be
updated.

You can always get an overview of all your Zenodo deposits using [the `list` and
`get` commands](get-and-list.qmd).
:::

Unlike the `publish` command, update only changes the metadata associated with
an existing deposit. The files in the deposit remain unchanged, and the existing
DOI is preserved.

The `update` command has three important arguments:

- `[METADATA_PATH]`: The path to the `.zenodo.toml` file. If no path is
  provided, it defaults to `.zenodo.toml` in the working directory.
- `--sandbox`: Update the deposit in the Zenodo sandbox instead of the main
  Zenodo website. This is useful for testing changes before updating a real
  deposit.
- `--draft`: Update the deposit without publishing the changes to the record.
  This allows you to review the updated deposit before publishing it.

For example, to update the metadata of a deposit using the default
`.zenodo.toml` file and without publishing the changes, run:

```bash {filename="Terminal"}
zen-do update --draft
```

To update a deposit in the sandbox, run:

```bash {filename="Terminal"}
zen-do update --sandbox
```

::: {.callout-tip}
By default, `update` asks for confirmation before making changes. To bypass this
prompt, for example in a CI/CD workflow, run:

```bash {filename="Terminal"}
zen-do update --yes
```
:::
